pages.caption: Illustrative image: Bio-based products  6028756933

pages.text: In the Netherlands, a company is producing a plant-based chemical building block for new bottles, films and fibres. This work helps the environment. It also creates new jobs. pages.text: The EU supports these ideas with money. EU research and innovation funding is helping some of these ideas move from the laboratory to the marketplace. Experts will meet in Dublin in 2026. They want to share knowledge and build new partnerships.

The October summit aims to advance the global bioeconomy by showcasing knowledge, promoting collaboration and building alliances. They hope to show that we can make products from nature. Together, they show how Europe is exploring ways to rely less on fossil raw materials, an approach that could also offer lessons to partners outside Europe.

pages.text: Europe is actively transitioning away from a reliance on fossil resources by embracing a circular bioeconomy. By utilizing renewable materials from land and sea, alongside agricultural residues, researchers are developing sustainable alternatives to products traditionally derived from oil and gas. Use renewable materials from land and sea, along with residues and by-products, to produce goods that now come from oil and gas.

pages.text: This shift is not merely environmental; it is an economic strategy designed to foster new industries and reduce dependence on imported materials. The European Union is heavily invested in this transition. This €2 billion public-private partnership supports Europe’s circular bioeconomy. Through initiatives like the Circular Bio-based Europe Joint Undertaking, the EU provides the necessary funding to bridge the gap between laboratory research and commercial production.

pages.text: The European Union is strategically pivoting toward a bio-based economy to mitigate its reliance on finite fossil raw materials. This transition involves the sophisticated conversion of organic waste, sewage sludge, and agricultural side streams into high-value commodities such as biopolymers, fertilizers, and chemical building blocks. Europe could use its food processing side streams, unavoidable food wastes and side streams from agriculture to help transition away from the fossil economy.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Bio-based products  6028756933

pages.text: By integrating these renewable feedstocks into industrial processes, the EU seeks to decouple economic growth from fossil fuel consumption. The economic implications of this transition are substantial. In 2023, biomass production and conversion employed about 17 million people in the EU and generated €863 billion in added value. To capitalize on this potential, the EU has implemented a comprehensive Bioeconomy Strategy, which prioritizes investment, market development, and international cooperation.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Showcasing bio-based products  6029613449

pages.text: The EU’s new Bioeconomy Strategy aims to build on this potential by encouraging investment, stronger markets for bio-based products and technologies, more sustainable supplies of biomass and international cooperation. The upcoming Global Bioeconomy Summit 2026 in Dublin serves as a critical nexus for this agenda. Alongside it, the International Bioeconomy Forum, which brings together government research and innovation experts from around the world, will hold its plenary meeting.

The summit will facilitate the launch of the Bio-based Europe Alliance and the International Bioeconomy Solutions Library, platforms designed to catalyze demand and disseminate technical expertise. As Professor Kevin O’Connor, chair of the scientific committee of the CBE JU, emphasizes, the challenge lies in scaling these laboratory-proven technologies to industrial levels.

“Europe could use its food processing side streams, unavoidable food wastes and side streams from agriculture to help transition away from the fossil economy,” said O’Connor, who chairs the scientific committee of the CBE JU. Ultimately, the success of this endeavor depends on aligning regulatory frameworks with the needs of a burgeoning green industry.

title: Making satellites easier to connect, repair and upgrade

pages.text: When you travel, you need many different plugs for your electronics. Space is the same. Satellites use many different connectors for power and data. This makes it hard to fix them. An international team created a new project called SPACE USB.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Satellite solar panels

pages.text: They want one standard plug for all satellites. This is like the USB ports we use on computers. It helps different parts connect easily. There are more than 16 000 satellites in space. When they stop working, we usually replace them.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Solar panels and satellite dish and chimney - Smaack - 201206

pages.text: This is expensive and creates space debris. If we can repair satellites, they will last longer. This also stops dangerous collisions in orbit. Researchers tested their new design with three other European interfaces. They showed that it works well with all of them.

This means standardisation is possible. A servicing spacecraft could visit a satellite to fix it or add new parts. This could help satellites stay in space for many more years instead of being thrown away.

evidence: The same, it turns out, is true in space, with spacecraft and satellites often using different connectors to transfer power, data and other services.
More than 16 000 satellites are now orbiting Earth, and the number continues to rise.
We were able to interconnect every device, showing that standardisation is possible.
A1-A2.headline: New Space Tools Help Repair Satellites

pages.text: Just as travelers often struggle with a variety of incompatible power plugs, the space industry faces a similar challenge. Spacecraft and satellites currently rely on diverse connectors to transfer power and data, which complicates maintenance. To address this, an international team launched the EU-funded SPACE USB project to develop a universal interface.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Satellite solar panels

pages.text: With more than 16 000 satellites currently orbiting Earth, the issue of sustainability is critical. When equipment becomes obsolete or fuel runs low, satellites are typically replaced, creating significant costs and increasing the risk of space debris. A single collision can scatter thousands of fragments, threatening other missions for decades.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Solar panels and satellite dish and chimney - Smaack - 201206

pages.text: By enabling in-orbit repairs, researchers hope to extend the operational life of these assets. The team successfully created a prototype called the Common Passive Interface. During testing, they demonstrated full compatibility with three existing European interfaces. This breakthrough proves that standardisation is possible, allowing a servicing vehicle to connect to and upgrade a satellite in orbit.

Such capabilities could eventually support in-space manufacturing and the construction of large structures. As European space policy shifts toward supporting repair and inspection missions, this universal connector could become a vital building block for a more sustainable and reusable space infrastructure.

Yet once a satellite runs out of fuel or its equipment becomes obsolete, it is generally replaced rather than repaired or upgraded in orbit.

B1-B2.headline: SPACE USB Makes Satellites Easier To Repair

pages.text: The lack of a unified interface in the aerospace sector mirrors the inconvenience of incompatible power adapters for terrestrial travelers. Currently, the absence of a standardized connection for power, data, and thermal management necessitates bespoke designs for every mission. The EU-funded SPACE USB project seeks to rectify this by introducing a universal interface, analogous to the ubiquitous USB standard in computing, to facilitate seamless connectivity across diverse satellite architectures.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Satellite solar panels

pages.text: The urgency of this initiative is underscored by the proliferation of orbital assets, with more than 16 000 satellites currently in operation. The prevailing paradigm of replacing rather than refurbishing obsolete or depleted spacecraft is economically inefficient and environmentally hazardous. Abandoned satellites often become space debris, posing a persistent collision risk that could jeopardize future missions for decades.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Solar panels and satellite dish and chimney - Smaack - 201206

pages.text: Implementing a standardized interface would enable in-orbit servicing, thereby extending the utility of existing hardware and mitigating the necessity for costly replacements. By late 2025, the research team had developed the Common Passive Interface, a prototype demonstrating mechanical and electrical compatibility with established European standards.

This development is pivotal for the emerging in-space services market, as evidenced by the joint declaration signed in 2026 by the European Commission and the European Space Agency. This policy shift supports the development of an infrastructure capable of inspection, repair, and modular assembly. Ultimately, the adoption of such a standard could transform the space economy, shifting from a model of disposal to one of persistent, serviceable, and modular orbital infrastructure.

Being able to service and repair satellites instead would extend their useful lives, avoid collision risks and reduce the need to launch costly replacements.

pages.text: Although public discourse frequently centers on outdoor air quality, the atmospheric conditions within our homes, schools, and workplaces have historically escaped rigorous scrutiny. Given that Europeans spend up to 90% of their lives indoors, the lack of awareness regarding indoor pollutants is significant. A consortium of EU-funded projects, including K-HEALTHinAIR and INQUIRE, is currently working to characterize these indoor environments and mitigate potential health risks.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Indoor Air Pollution  5456651785

pages.text: The challenge lies in the nature of indoor pollution; most contaminants are odorless and difficult to detect, leading occupants to adapt to their presence. Researchers have identified an immense diversity of chemical pollutants, ranging from particulate matter generated by cooking and smoking to complex chemical signatures found in household dust. Pernilla Bohlin Nizzetto, coordinator of the INQUIRE project, emphasizes that household dust acts as a chemical fingerprint of the home, often containing substances released from consumer products.

pages.text: Her team’s analysis of 200 homes revealed measurable biological effects, including impacts on lung cells and hormone-related markers. Children, who spend considerable time in contact with floor surfaces, are identified as a particularly vulnerable demographic. The research underscores that while some chemicals may not cause immediate illness, they can have long-term neurological or hormonal consequences. To combat this, scientists are developing innovative monitoring technologies and evidence-based guidelines.

pages.text: These include air quality simulators and filtration systems. The researchers argue that improving indoor air quality requires a paradigm shift, moving from individual actions—such as improved ventilation—to a comprehensive policy framework that integrates health, building standards, and environmental regulations. By treating the home as a chemical reactor, policymakers can begin to address the invisible pollution that defines our daily lives.

title: Open source tech helps farmers put more trust in digital tools

pages.text: Farmers want to use new technology. But they need to know it works. A farmer trusts a neighbor more than a far-away company. Nikos Marianos works with a group called OpenAgri. They want to help farmers trust digital tools.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Low cost precision farming

pages.text: The team has researchers from many countries. They work until the end of 2026. They do not make just one app. They make open-source parts. Companies can use these parts to build better tools for farmers.

imageProvenance.credit: Prem Rajak, Abhratanu Ganguly, Satadal Adhikary, Suchandra Bhattacharya / Wikimedia Commons

pages.text: Christopher Brewster is a leader in the project. He says it is like building with Lego. You can change the parts to fit your farm. The tools can help with weather, water, and pests. They also talk to each other.

The team made a new web app called a Decision Support Tool. It helps farmers compare different tools. They can see if a tool works with bad internet or if it costs too much. This helps farmers make good choices.

evidence: Farmers want to innovate, but they need to see the benefits.
Marianos is working with researchers from Belgium, Cyprus, France, Greece, the Netherlands, Poland and Serbia on an EU-funded initiative called OpenAgri.
The work runs until the end of 2026.
A1-A2.headline: Open Tools Help Farmers Trust Technology

pages.text: Convincing farmers to invest in digital agriculture is a challenge. According to Nikos Marianos of the Greek hub GreenSupplyChain, farmers need to see technology working in familiar conditions. A recommendation from a neighbor often carries more weight than a distant demonstration.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Low cost precision farming

pages.text: To address this, the EU-funded OpenAgri initiative is creating a new way to evaluate digital tools. Running until the end of 2026, the project involves researchers from several countries. Instead of building new apps from scratch, they provide open-source building blocks that companies can adapt to specific needs.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Applications of integrated IoT and smart sensors for precision farming

imageProvenance.credit: Prem Rajak, Abhratanu Ganguly, Satadal Adhikary, Suchandra Bhattacharya / Wikimedia Commons

pages.text: Christopher Brewster, the project coordinator, compares this to building with Lego. These components handle tasks like irrigation, pest risk, and reporting. Crucially, they are designed to communicate with one another, solving a common problem where apps operate in isolation. The project’s main output is a Decision Support Tool (DST).

This free web app allows farmers and advisers to compare solutions based on real evidence. Users can check how a tool performs with poor internet, its energy consumption, and its overall cost. By involving farmers in the design process, the team ensures that the technology addresses actual farming problems rather than just sales pitches.

evidence: What matters, according to Nikos Marianos, managing director at Greek digital innovation hub GreenSupplyChain, is seeing evidence that a technology works in conditions farmers recognise.

Rather than designing yet another farming app, the OpenAgri team provides smaller companies and start-ups with open-source building blocks they can adapt to farmers’ needs, without building every component from scratch.
The researchers’ most comprehensive creation so far is a Decision Support Tool (DST).
B1-B2.headline: Open Source Tech Helps Farmers Trust Tools

pages.text: The adoption of digital agriculture often hinges on trust. As Nikos Marianos, managing director of the Greek innovation hub GreenSupplyChain, observes, farmers are understandably skeptical of digital solutions that lack proof of efficacy in local environments. For a farmer, a successful demonstration on a neighboring plot is far more persuasive than a generic sales pitch.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Low cost precision farming

pages.text: Marianos, who has spent 15 years at the intersection of agriculture and technology, emphasizes that bridging this trust gap is essential for innovation. The EU-funded OpenAgri initiative, which runs until the end of 2026, seeks to provide this evidence. By collaborating with researchers across Europe, the project aims to move beyond guesswork. Rather than developing redundant applications, the team provides open-source building blocks that developers can customize.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Applications of integrated IoT and smart sensors for precision farming

imageProvenance.credit: Prem Rajak, Abhratanu Ganguly, Satadal Adhikary, Suchandra Bhattacharya / Wikimedia Commons

pages.text: Christopher Brewster, the project coordinator from Maastricht University, likens this modular approach to building with Lego, where components can be combined or replaced to meet specific regional requirements. A central achievement of the project is the Decision Support Tool (DST), a web-based application designed to help stakeholders evaluate digital solutions. The DST allows users to compare tools based on practical metrics, such as energy efficiency, cost, and performance in areas with limited connectivity.

This evidence-based approach is vital, as many existing agricultural applications fail to communicate with one another. By prioritizing interoperability, the OpenAgri team ensures that services—ranging from weather monitoring to disease risk assessment—can exchange data seamlessly. Beyond technical development, the project emphasizes community engagement. By involving farmers in the design process across 14 pilot sites, the researchers ensure that the software addresses genuine agricultural challenges.

While the project faces the long-term challenge of maintaining these open-source tools after funding concludes, the integration of its services into the Linux Foundation’s AgStack initiative suggests a sustainable path forward. Ultimately, the project aims to democratize access to technology, narrowing the digital divide between farmers who can afford advanced systems and those who cannot.

evidence: He knows how hard it can be to convince farmers to invest without clear evidence.
Crucially, they are designed to communicate with each other – something many existing agricultural applications struggle to do.
Users can compare practical factors, including how a tool copes with poor internet, how much energy it uses, what it costs to run, and how it holds up in different farming conditions.

pages.text: Roland Séférian works at the National Centre for Meteorological Research in France. He designs models to study future climate change. The IPCC uses models to show how the Earth system works. These models use large grid cells.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Funding for climate research in the natural and technical sciences versus the social sciences and humanities

imageProvenance.credit: Authors of the study: Indra Overland, Benjamin K.Sovacool / Wikimedia Commons

pages.text: This makes it hard to see climate risks in small places. Researchers in Europe are making new models. They want to see how human activities change the climate. They also want to see climate processes better.

The ESM2025 project studied how the Earth absorbs and releases carbon. Researchers worked together to improve these models. They looked at land carbon storage and ocean circulation. New tools like AI help improve these models. Researchers also use NextGEMS to see local details.

Traditional models use grid squares of 150 kilometres. NextGEMS uses a scale of a few kilometres. This helps people understand risks like heat or drought in their own towns. It helps leaders make better plans for the future.

evidence: Working at the National Centre for Meteorological Research (CNRM), the climate scientist designs models that project future climate change.
These models simulate the entire Earth system by dividing it into a grid of large boxes, known as grid cells.
Alongside these refinements, new tools, including AI, are helping to improve climate models.
A1-A2.headline: New Climate Models Show Local Risks

pages.text: Climate scientist Roland Séférian, based at the National Centre for Meteorological Research in Toulouse, is refining how we project future climate change. Current models, such as those used by the IPCC, divide the Earth into large grid cells. While useful for global averages, these models often struggle to capture smaller-scale processes that define regional climate risks.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Funding for climate research in the natural and technical sciences versus the social sciences and humanities

imageProvenance.credit: Authors of the study: Indra Overland, Benjamin K.Sovacool / Wikimedia Commons

pages.text: To address this, European researchers launched the ESM2025 project, which ran from 2021 until November 2025. This initiative improved how models represent the interactions between the atmosphere, land, and oceans. By refining these links, scientists can better track how human emissions and land use affect the environment. For instance, the team discovered that rivers transport around 20% more carbon to the oceans than previously estimated.

Furthermore, the integration of AI has allowed for more consistent simulations of complex natural cycles. Complementing this work, the NextGEMS project has introduced a new generation of models. While traditional models rely on 150-kilometre grid squares, NextGEMS can simulate climate processes at a scale of just a few kilometres.

This high-resolution approach provides essential data for local decision-makers. By understanding local wind patterns or rainfall, communities can better prepare for climate-related challenges like wildfires or extreme heat. These advancements ensure that regions previously excluded from climate narratives are now part of the global conversation.
